description: We’re two high school robotics students passionate about aerospace and building real-world solutions. For the MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge, we’re creating a tool that reconciles fire detections from both satellites, matching coarse 1 km pixels with sharper 375 m data into one consistent map. Our goal: fewer missed fires, fewer false alarms, and clearer data for wildfire responders.
summary:
FireLens is an interactive satellite fire intelligence platform that brings together NASA's MODIS and VIIRS observations to provide a clearer, more scientifically meaningful picture of historical burning activity. Although both instruments detect active fires, differences in their spatial resolution, sensitivity, and observation timing can make long-term comparisons misleading.

Rather than simply plotting hotspots on a map, FireLens focuses on understanding these differences and making them clear to users. Our platform brings together interactive geographic maps, historical activity calendars, and sensor-specific comparisons in one research workspace. Users can explore regional fire patterns, examine seasonal trends, trace observations back to their original datasets, and export findings for further analysis.

We also designed FireLens to work across different geographic regions without requiring major changes to the underlying system. By making it easier to compare and interpret satellite observations, FireLens can help researchers, land managers, and emergency planners better understand historical fire activity and use that information to guide their decisions.
details:
NASA has been collecting satellite observations of fire activity for decades, but we realized that comparing these records over time isn't as straightforward as it seems. MODIS and VIIRS, two of the main instruments used to detect fires, have different resolutions, sensitivities, and observation schedules. VIIRS can detect smaller heat sources that MODIS might miss, which means that simply combining their records could make burning activity appear to increase even when part of that change comes from the instruments themselves.

We developed FireLens to make these historical observations more comparable and useful. FireLens brings together over 25 years of NASA FIRMS data into an interactive web application where users can explore burning activity across the United States and the Iberian Peninsula. Behind the interface, we built a processing system that organizes observations into consistent spatial grids, accounts for differences between satellites, and uses statistical calibration to estimate activity on a common scale. We also account for gaps in satellite observations so that missing data isn't mistaken for an absence of fires.

One of our most interesting findings came from comparing historical trends before and after harmonization. In the United States, simply switching from raw MODIS to VIIRS records produces an apparent 72% increase per decade. After harmonization, that trend is approximately zero. The first comparison is intentionally invalid, but the difference demonstrates why accounting for changing instruments matters. We also tested our calibration methods against historical MODIS observations and built an Evidence Lab where users can examine the results, uncertainty, and limitations themselves.

We wanted FireLens to be more than a tool that displays a historical fire calendar. Users can investigate seasonal patterns, identify unusual months, explore where MODIS and VIIRS disagree, and see how harmonization changes their interpretation of the data. We also connected the analysis to documented wildfire events and developed additional research features for Texas and California. Our Texas case study, for example, examines the exceptional burning activity of April 2011 and how the region's long-term trends change after accounting for satellite differences. Users can download the underlying data and generate regional reports that combine historical patterns, unusual periods, and supporting evidence.

We built FireLens using React, TypeScript, JavaScript, Node.js, Vite, and H3 spatial indexing, with NASA FIRMS satellite observations providing the foundation for our analysis. We developed our own data-processing and statistical calibration pipeline, used Vitest and Playwright to test both the scientific calculations and application functionality, and deployed the finished platform through Vercel.

Throughout development, we had to consider differences in satellite coverage, missing observations, geographic scale, and uncertainty. We also made sure to distinguish satellite-detected burning activity from burned area or the number of individual wildfires, since those measurements aren't interchangeable.

Our goal is to help researchers, fire managers, and other users draw more reliable conclusions from historical satellite observations. Rather than predicting where the next wildfire will occur FireLens helps people understand how burning activity has changed, recognize unusual historical patterns, and evaluate how much confidence they should place in the data they're using.
